claim: Humans agree well on finding major claims and premises in essays (kappa .877 and .833) but poorly on plain claims (kappa .635, unitized alpha .524). Claim boundary is the weak point of standardisation.
agent_test: Have the agent mark claim/premise spans on essays; compare its span agreement with itself across 3 samples at equal tokens. Expect the same weak spot on claim vs premise.

claim: Agreement on Toulmin-style structure falls sharply outside clean essays: alpha_U .48 overall on web discourse, .59-.69 in comments/forums but .22-.24 in articles/blogs, and .08-.68 by topic.
agent_test: Score agent restatements on clean vs messy text separately; do not assume essay accuracy transfers.

claim: A joint model that links components and relations beats separate classifiers (claim F1 +.071, linked-pair F1 +.077); the machine reached 95.2% of human F1 on components but only 87.9% on relations and 80.5% on stance.
agent_test: Compare one-pass list components then links then stance vs separate calls at equal tokens on link recall.

claim: Attack relations are systematically harder than support for both pre-LLM and LLM systems (attack stance F1 .413 in ILP; attack F1 below support in nearly all LLM datasets; Nixon-Kennedy Llama-13B attack F1 12). Gap search: on UKP essays a confidence-gated second pass raised attack F1 from .383 to .427 (14% of pairs debated; 42 attack test items; not significance-tested); debating all pairs gave .378 (d06).
agent_test: Measure agent attack-link recall on a held-out set; add a dedicated counter-argument pass and see if it moves.
audit_note: The Llama-13B attack F1 of 12 is on Nixon-Kennedy (CDCP has only support labels, so its attack F1 is undefined '-'); other numbers match Stab and Gurevych .413, Gorur et al., and Baba and Chudziak.
claim_before_audit: Attack relations are systematically harder than support for both pre-LLM and LLM systems (attack stance F1 .413 in ILP; attack F1 below support in nearly all LLM datasets; CDCP Llama-13B attack F1 12). Gap search: on UKP essays a confidence-gated second pass raised attack F1 from .383 to .427 (14% of pairs debated; 42 attack test items; not significance-tested); debating all pairs gave .378 (d06).

claim: The linked-versus-convergent distinction is contested in theory: some authors say it need not be drawn for structure identification (Freeman: ambiguous; Yanal: equals one vs several arguments; Conway: linked can be omitted), while the Pirozelli et al. pipeline rated its grouping 2.85 of 3. Gap search: no study measures whether the label changes a downstream answer; giving an LLM extracted argument structure raised F1 only .2525 to .2647 (Qwen3.6:27B) on persuasion prediction (d05).
agent_test: Run agent with and without a linked/convergent label and test whether the label changes final-answer accuracy or only the diagram. Use the drop-one-premise test (a07).

claim: A practical test for linked premises: remove or falsify one premise and ask if the conclusion still follows. Rabbit and Holding Hands rules locate missing premises by term matching. Taught method; no accuracy data.
agent_test: After drafting a restatement, drop each premise and mark which collapse the claim. Count how often removal changes the answer.

claim: Hidden-premise recovery by people: 79.8% on ARCT warrant choice, 90.9% with formal reasoning training; education alone negligible; topic familiarity not significant.
agent_test: Human baseline of about 80%; not directly testable on the agent.

claim: BERT's 77% on ARCT was a cue artefact: warrants alone gave 71%, the word not predicts the label 61% of the time, and on an adversarial set accuracy fell to 53% (mean and median 50%; 5 of 20 seeds failed to train). Hidden-premise benchmarks can be gamed by surface cues. Numbers re-checked in the paper text.
agent_test: Always test the agent on adversarial ARCT (warrants swapped, claim negated) and report both numbers.

claim: A zero-shot single LLM (79.28%) beats a fine-tuned RoBERTa (75.64%) and an LSTM (70.5%) on the ARCT test set (baselines reproduced by Ku et al.), whereas the original 2018 systems were near chance (.556-.560).
agent_test: Reproduce a single zero-shot run on adversarial ARCT, since the original is cue-prone.
audit_note: 'Far exceed' is too strong against the stronger neural baselines: zero-shot LLM 79.28 beats RoBERTa 75.64 by only 3.6 points and LSTM 70.5 by 8.8; only the original 2018 systems (.556-.560) were near chance.
claim_before_audit: Modern LLMs far exceed early neural models on warrant choice: zero-shot single LLM 79.28% vs RoBERTa 75.64% and LSTM 70.5% on ARCT test; early systems were near chance (.556-.560).

claim: Two debating LLM agents that each pick their own stance on the missing premise lift ARCT accuracy to 86.94% (sequential) and 84.46% (simultaneous) over 79.28%; assigned stances make it worse than a single agent.
agent_test: Compare self-chosen-stance two-pass vs single pass at equal tokens, plus a token-matched single pass sampled twice (not in the paper).

claim: Writing intermediate (implicit) premises before a logic check raises entailment accuracy up to 3 steps on ANLI (.496 to .716) and ARCT (.276 to .560); on Microtext 4 steps peak at .555 with a drop at 5 (chance .333). One author group, one engine. Gap search (d10): re-read; only ANLI and ARCT, 1 to 3 steps, two fixed candidate premises, AMR+SAT checker. Not tested on math, planning or code, so the peak at 3 to 4 is not shown outside entailment sets.
agent_test: Bound hidden-premise steps at 1 to 5 at matched tokens; look for a peak near 3 to 4.

claim: LLM-written warrants were judged acceptable more often than dataset gold warrants for GPT-4 (61.7% vs 45.7%) but not for Llama-2-70B (26.3%); annotator agreement was very low (kappa .18-.31), so this is weak evidence.
agent_test: Use two independent judges and report agreement before trusting hidden-premise quality.

claim: Prompting with the theory name (according to Toulmin model) makes models emit claim, grounds and warrant (success 99-100% GPT-4, 35-42.5% Falcon-40B); naming Toulmin beats Walton or Freeman, tied to pretraining frequency (C4 mentions 3401, 975, 66). Success counted term presence only, not correctness.
agent_test: Compare a Toulmin-labelled restatement template vs plain what-is-the-claim at equal tokens, and check parts are correct.

claim: Strong LLMs do few-shot argument component classification near or above older trained models: GPT-4 with 5 nearest-neighbour examples macro F1 .836 vs .826 Stab and Gurevych; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 passes .857; explicit structural features hurt in-context learning.
agent_test: Retrieved similar examples vs fixed examples in the restatement step at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: the .836 vs .821 comparison in the table is for different ensemble rows but the paper text does state structural features were counter-productive in ICL; Potash .849 and Kuribayashi .856 are above GPT-4, so 'near or above' is apt; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 reached 0.863.

claim: Small open models are unreliable: Llama-2-13B falls below random on most zero-shot argument mining tasks; with under 10 demonstrations larger models match BERT-type models trained on 500 samples.
agent_test: Not testable; our agent uses a strong model.

claim: Relation classification (support/attack between two texts) is dataset-sensitive: Llama-70B 96 vs RoBERTa 90 on Debatepedia/Procon but 64-68 vs 56-62 on Nixon-Kennedy (and 73 vs 67 macro on Microtexts); on essays Llama-70B attack F1 is only 52.
agent_test: Evaluate on at least two corpora; do not tune on microtexts only.
audit_note: In Gorur et al. Table 1 (checked by cell coordinates) 96/95/96 for Llama-70B belongs to Debatepedia/Procon (RoBERTa 90/89/90); on Microtexts Llama-70B is 81/52/73 vs RoBERTa 73/53/67.
claim_before_audit: Relation classification (support/attack between two texts) is dataset-sensitive: Llama-70B 96 vs RoBERTa 67 on Microtexts, but 64-68 vs 56-62 on Nixon-Kennedy; essays attack F1 only 52.

claim: Prompt format changes LLM argument-mining scores about as much as the task (GPT-4 AM 64.5 concrete vs 70.6 symbolic; binary-matrix output 9.88 F1, below random); chain-of-thought makes results robust to format (p about .77 vs <.05 without CoT).
agent_test: Run restatement in 2-3 output formats (prose, JSON, indexed list) and report variance.

claim: Voting over four paraphrased prompts adds 2.4 to 4.5 points on stance classification (GPT-5.2 78.0% UKP, 91.9% Args.me); self-rated certainty is unreliable; CoT effect is mixed. The same paper appears under two author lists (a15 Gampel, c12 Pietron).
agent_test: Same-token voting over paraphrased restatements vs one long restatement.

claim: A ten-step GPT pipeline reconstructs textbook argument graphs well (conclusion accuracy 92.5%, span F1 75.7, relation accuracy 80.57%, human ratings 2.85-2.96 of 3) but does badly on public corpora with exact span match (AbstRCT link F1 20.82 vs 39.74; AAEC 0.41 vs 55.72). With gold components AbstRCT link F1 is 51.51 but AAEC only 22.88, so span finding is the main but not the only bottleneck. Numbers re-checked in the paper.
agent_test: Evaluate span finding and linking separately (give gold spans to isolate each).

claim: Argument reconstruction as training data helps some reasoning tasks (ReClor 78.28 to 84.48 on Qwen3-4B) not others (WebisCMV20 55.45 to 53.30); about 41% of premises are implicit; LLMs write fewer implicit premises than humans; fallacies, LLM-written text and arguments over 290 words or 9+ premises hurt.
agent_test: Test whether restating arguments of more than 9 premises degrades answers vs chunking.

claim: Fallacy reconstruction: GPT-4 finds a right fallacy at P@1 in 57% of arguments (Arg@6 89.0%, Llama-2 59.7%); models over-predict False Equivalence; writing the hidden premise helps GPT-4 but not Llama-2.
agent_test: Check whether the agent's hidden-premise step exposes fallacies better than direct fallacy naming.

claim: A Toulmin-based critical-question loop (plan as premises/conclusion, 8 questions, need 7/8 yes) lifted LLM-judge MT-Bench scores: Llama 3.1-70B reasoning 8.05 to 8.4, math 8.95 to 9.55 (re-checked in the paper). But Nemotron-51B reasoning CoT (7.7) beat CQoT (7.3), a plan-plus-answer ablation keeps part of the gain, and there is no token-matched control. Gap search (d08): re-read, no sample-and-vote baseline and no non-LLM judge; generation settings allow 8192 new tokens for the pipeline vs 2000 for the baseline. Critical-question generation itself is under 57% useful for 11 zero-shot LLMs (d09).
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of CQoT vs plain CoT vs sample-and-vote.

claim: Showing an LLM-built argument map to users cut over-trust and improved error correction on hard verbal items (b=-0.199 and +0.182, p=.002, N=204); the map had structural faults in 5 of 180 rationales (2.8%).
agent_test: Relevant only if the agent shows maps to a user.

claim: Argument-diagram training raises reasoning scores in humans, but size depends on the test. Primary source opened: Cullen et al. 2018 (Princeton, N=105 seminar vs 56 control, quasi-experiment) found d=0.71 [0.37, 1.04] on LSAT logical reasoning and d=0.87 on blind-graded essays; weekly feedback is confounded with diagramming. They report that recent studies using both tests found effects about three times smaller on LSAT than on CCTST. Earlier figures (0.8 SD, 0.34 SD, Twardy, Alvarez, van Gelder) were still not opened.
agent_test: Not testable on the agent.

claim: Standardisation recipe: remove noise, restate questions, clarify vague claims, recover unstated parts with the logically minimal (weakest) bridging premise; indicator words are neither necessary nor sufficient.
agent_test: Test a weakest-bridging-premise instruction vs unconstrained hidden premise on whether added premises are rated acceptable.
audit_note: Minor: SEP says charity can favour the logically minimum premise rather than mandating it; Davies et al. is a practitioner method (rabbit rule) not the SEP recipe itself.

claim: Still no opened study tests whether restating a claim with its grounds improves an agent's downstream answer accuracy at equal tokens. Nearest evidence says structure buys faithfulness and inspectability, not accuracy: Toulmin-form training gave no accuracy gain over plain SFT-CoT (32.67 vs 32.14, Llama-3.1-8B, d04); extracted argument structure barely moved zero-shot LLMs (d05); verdicts computed from generated arguments did not beat direct prediction (d11). Only TRACE links Toulmin-shaped reasoning to accuracy (r=.741 across models; GSM8K 77.86 to 84.69 with TRACE reward in one 1.5B run, d03).
agent_test: Central experiment: with/without a restate-claim-with-grounds step on a reasoning benchmark at equal tokens.

claim: Independent human study: a 12-week argument-diagramming seminar gave a gain of d=0.71 on LSAT logical reasoning over controls (N=105 vs 56, quasi-experimental, Princeton), essays d=0.87.
agent_test: Not testable on the agent. Useful only as a prior that explicit structure helps people with feedback.

claim: Toulmin-style structure in an LLM trace correlates with accuracy across models (TRACE r=.741, n=273 model-benchmark pairs, 26.3K traces) and as a GRPO reward lifted GSM8K from 77.86 to 84.69 over an accuracy+length reward on a 1.5B model; one run, model size confounds the correlation.
agent_test: Label the agent's own steps (claim, evidence, warrant, rebuttal) and check whether structure score predicts correctness within one model at fixed length.

claim: Making answers Toulmin-shaped improves inspectability but not accuracy: CGCL TrustScore 72.89 vs SFT-CoT 60.86 while accuracy was 32.67 vs 32.14 (Llama-3.1-8B, MedCaseReasoning); LLM-judged scores built by the same authors.
agent_test: Compare a Toulmin-format answer vs free CoT at equal tokens on accuracy and on a human audit of the reasoning.

claim: An LLM reviewer used as the only gate on an argument graph finds injected structural defects at .96 to 1.00 recall but objects to 9.8% of correct graphs, flips verdict on 6.2% of identical inputs and takes 2,758 ms vs 1 ms; deterministic checks (schema, cycles, dangling links, span match) are exact.
agent_test: After restating, run code checks for orphan premises, cycles and unquoted spans before any model review.

claim: Debate or a second pass helps only on uncertain items: gating at confidence 0.70 (14% of pairs) gave macro F1 .585 vs .561 for full debate, net +36 fixes; debating all gave 249 fixes vs 236 regressions. Same pattern in an 8B shared-task winner (retrieval constraint plus selective debate).
agent_test: Run the extra attack-finding pass only when first-pass confidence is low; compare with an always-on pass at equal tokens.

claim: Long text is handled by chunking to sentence-level units with an anchor (scientific entities), not by one global restatement; human gold alpha .80, silver LLM-ensemble labels beat the small gold set for fine-tuning. No direct measure of a length cliff (over 290 words, 9+ premises) was found.
agent_test: Restate one long argument whole vs chunked, at equal tokens; score premise recall.

claim: Open after gap search: no source scores a current LLM on adversarial ARCT, no source checks that Toulmin parts are correct (not just present), and no source runs CQoT against sample-and-vote at equal tokens. arXiv API, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and WebSearch were rate-limited or out of budget.
agent_test: Run the adversarial ARCT set on the agent model; run token-matched CoT and self-consistency next to any critical-question loop.
